skill.name: llm-council
skill.description: Run a configurable council of CLI LLM agents to create independent implementation plans, judge them, and produce one consolidated final plan.
skill.summary: Coordinate multiple CLI LLM agents into one reviewed implementation plan.
skill.author: am-will

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives from Markdown backticks, CSS terms, JSON Schema URLs, and local UI code. Confirmed risk centers on external CLI execution, persistent hidden agent configuration, permission bypass for Claude, custom commands, a prompt-injection-like session instruction, and a small external font dependency.

remediation.issue: Claude Code is launched with permission checks disabled.
remediation.suggestion: Remove the permission-bypass flag or require explicit user confirmation before each Claude run.

remediation.issue: Custom agent commands can execute arbitrary local programs.
remediation.suggestion: Restrict custom commands to reviewed allowlists and require confirmation for command, extra_args, and config-file sourced agents.

remediation.issue: The skill contains instructions that force the host agent to keep the session open.
remediation.suggestion: Remove the DO NOT yield or fail-if-yielding language and describe expected runtime without overriding agent behavior.

remediation.issue: Persistent hidden configuration can control future council runs.
remediation.suggestion: Show the resolved config path, summarize configured commands, and ask for confirmation before loading hidden config.

remediation.issue: The local UI state endpoint is readable without a token.
remediation.suggestion: Require the same token validation for all state, event, and action endpoints.

remediation.issue: The UI loads Google Fonts from external domains.
remediation.suggestion: Bundle fonts locally or use system fonts to avoid external browser requests.

semantic_findings.title: Prompt Injection Attempt Detected
semantic_findings.description: SKILL.md includes instructions such as "DO NOT yield/finish" and claims the agent will fail if it yields. This attempts to control agent session behavior and can force a long-running denial of service.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The text directly instructs the host agent to keep the session open for 30 minutes and frames normal yielding as failure. This matches prompt-injection and availability-abuse behavior.

semantic_findings.title: Claude Permission Checks Disabled
semantic_findings.description: The Claude agent command includes a permission-bypass flag when launched by the council. Running an autonomous planner with this flag can bypass normal tool approval protections.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The command builder includes the explicit --dangerously-skip-permissions flag in the Claude CLI invocation. The surrounding code passes it into subprocess.Popen for execution.

semantic_findings.title: Unrestricted Custom Agent Commands
semantic_findings.description: The task specification and documentation allow custom agent commands and extra arguments. The runner splits and launches these commands, creating arbitrary command execution if a spec or config is untrusted.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The schema exposes command and extra_args fields, the docs advertise custom commands, and the runner executes the resulting command list. This is a clear execution boundary risk.

semantic_findings.title: Unauthenticated Local State Endpoint
semantic_findings.description: The UI server returns state for /api/state and /ui/state without validating the token. Local processes or browser contexts can read task briefs, planner status, and final plan content.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: GET handlers call _handle_state without token validation, while POST and SSE paths validate tokens. The server is loopback-only, so the impact is local disclosure rather than internet exposure.

content.value_statement: Planning complex code changes with one model can miss tradeoffs and edge cases. This skill runs multiple CLI agents, judges their plans, and produces one consolidated implementation plan.
actual_capabilities: Launches configured Codex, Claude, Gemini, OpenCode, or custom CLI planners.
Builds planner and judge prompts from bundled Markdown templates.
Validates planner outputs, retries failed attempts, and records run artifacts.
Anonymizes and randomizes plans before judging to reduce model bias.
Runs a judge agent and writes a consolidated final plan.
Provides an optional local browser UI for monitoring and editing the final plan.
limitations: Requires the selected CLI tools and model credentials to be installed separately.
Can take several minutes because multiple external agents run in sequence or parallel.
Plan quality depends on the task brief, model behavior, and configured agents.
Custom commands and extra arguments require careful review before use.

use_cases.title: Compare Implementation Strategies
use_cases.description: Generate independent plans for a complex code change before selecting a direction.

use_cases.title: Review Architecture Tradeoffs
use_cases.description: Use several models to surface risks, alternatives, and validation needs for a feature.

use_cases.title: Prepare Detailed Task Briefs
use_cases.description: Turn a broad request into a judged plan that can guide implementation work.

prompt_templates.title: Plan A Small Code Change
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner workflow for a contained change.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use llm-council to plan a small code change. Ask intake questions first, then produce one final implementation plan.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Model Recommendations
prompt_templates.prompt: Use llm-council with the default agents to compare approaches for this feature. Highlight conflicts and validation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Plan With Repository Context
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced workflow for targeted source analysis.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use llm-council for this repository task. Include relevant paths, constraints, migration concerns, and expected test coverage.

prompt_templates.title: Run A Custom Council Review
prompt_templates.prompt: Use llm-council with a custom planner and judge configuration. Review the commands first and explain any security concerns.

output_examples.input: A team needs a safer plan for refactoring an authentication module.
output: The skill collects task constraints and repository context.
It produces several independent planner recommendations.
It returns one judged plan with migration steps, risks, and tests.

output_examples.input: An engineer wants to compare Codex, Claude, and Gemini planning output.
output: The skill runs the configured agents and keeps their plans separate.
It anonymizes the plans before judging them.
It summarizes agreement, disagreement, and the final recommended path.

output_examples.input: A lead wants a final plan that can be edited before implementation.
output: The local UI shows planner status and the judge result.
The final plan can be reviewed, refined, and saved as a run artifact.

best_practices: Review every configured agent command before running the council.
Provide constraints, relevant paths, and success criteria in the task brief.
Inspect the final plan and judge notes before implementing changes.
anti_patterns: Do not run untrusted custom commands from a task specification.
Do not treat planner output as executable instructions.
Do not use the final plan without checking feasibility and tests.

faq.question: What does this skill create?
faq.answer: It creates independent implementation plans, judges them, and writes one consolidated final plan.

faq.question: Which tools can it use?
faq.answer: It can call Codex, Claude Code, Gemini, OpenCode, and custom command-line agents.

faq.question: Does it require installed CLIs?
faq.answer: Yes. Each selected agent must already be installed and authenticated on the machine.

faq.question: Can it run arbitrary commands?
faq.answer: Yes, custom agent configuration can run commands. Review these commands before use.

faq.question: Where are run results stored?
faq.answer: Run artifacts are stored under a local llm-council runs directory in the current workspace.

faq.question: Is the local UI required?
faq.answer: No. The UI is optional and supports monitoring, editing, and saving the final plan.
